description: Hello, we are a team of computer science students—from both engineering and bachelor’s degree programs—who have participated in challenges, and we are ready for the next one.
summary:
Martians is an educational, pixel-art video game for children. The player joins the crew of the Ares 1 base in Arcadia Planitia—a region on Mars with subsurface ice that is currently being studied for future human missions. First, the player chooses a profession: engineer, biologist, doctor, or astrophysicist. They must then survive for 60 sols (Martian days) by managing solar energy, navigating storms, tending to crops, and addressing challenges such as hunger, fatigue, radiation exposure, and physical health.

To ensure a realistic experience, we incorporated actual data from NASA into the game’s mechanics. This includes physiological data on astronauts (such as muscle and bone loss, and the effects of sleep and nutrition), information on plant growth in space, radiation measurements from the Martian surface, and meteorological data—including the impact of dust storms on solar panels.

Players learn how each system works through various minigames: repairing solar panels, planting and watering potatoes, exercising, undergoing medical check-ups, extracting ice, and analyzing samples. A robotic guide named A.R.I.A. explains key concepts through brief, accessible messages.

This project is significant because it translates the real science behind human exploration of Mars into decisions that children can understand and make themselves, while sparking their interest in STEM fields.
details:
What does it do?

Martians: Mission Ares 1 is an educational survival game for kids aged 7–12. The player chooses a role (engineer, biologist, doctor or astrophysicist) and has to keep their crew alive for 60 sols on Mars. They manage solar energy, dust storms, potato crops, hunger, fatigue, radiation and physical fitness through mini-games: repairing panels, farming, exercising, medical check-ups, drilling for ice and analyzing samples in the lab. A robot guide, A.R.I.A., explains each concept in short, kid-friendly messages.

Real NASA data behind the game

The game's rules come from real data, turned into game values:

  • Location, Arcadia Planitia: NASA studies this region as a candidate landing site for humans. The SHARAD radar on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter found large buried ice sheets there. NASA's 2019 "treasure map" of water ice, built from MRO and Mars Odyssey data, shows ice only centimeters below the surface. The NASA-funded SWIM project maps this ice to help choose future landing sites. The region is also low and flat, which makes landing safer, and it gets more sunlight than the poles. The game's backgrounds are based on real maps of the area. That is why ice is at the center of the game: players drill it, analyze it and explore ice mounds.
  • Physiological data: the effects of sleep, nutrition and low gravity on astronauts drive the crew's hunger, fatigue and physical fitness, and explain why they need to exercise every day.
  • Plant data: research on growing crops determines which plant is grown and harvested.
  • Radiation data: radiation on the Martian surface affects astronauts differently depending on how much shielding they have, and that determines how much damage they build up.
  • Weather data: Martian dust storms and the way they cut sunlight set how often storms happen, how dirty the panels get and how much power they produce.

Benefits and impact

Kids learn the real challenges of human life on Mars (energy, food, radiation and health) by making decisions and seeing their consequences. Neglecting sleep, food or exercise makes every task harder, just like on a real mission. We hope schools, museums and science workshops will use the game to spark interest in STEM and space careers.

Tools

Godot Engine 4 (GDScript), Python (NumPy and Pillow) for our asset-processing scripts, JSON for the game rules and content, Google Gemini to generate AI base art (processed and adapted by the team), Claude for code generation, ElevenLabs for sounds and music, and Git/GitHub for teamwork

Creativity and factors considered

The game turns real scientific data into mechanics a child can feel, and it is set in a real candidate landing site (Arcadia Planitia) instead of a generic Mars. Each role plays differently, the way work is split in a real crew, and the systems are connected: a storm dirties the panels, lowers the power and makes everything else harder. We designed it for children (short texts, simple controls, learning by doing) and simplified the science without losing accuracy.
